topic: Entry with a skeptical head coach
stem: A minor-league baseball club has hired a consultant, and the general manager has told field manager Bogdan Dudek why. Over a long breakfast, Dudek talks about how he runs a team and what he wants from his players; when the consultant sums it up, he says, "That's it exactly." Then he shrugs. "The last one had slides and studies. Nice fella. I never saw one of my guys do anything different." Which step would best build a working relationship with Dudek now?
options: Ask how he coaches and what he wants from his players
Give him a short summary of research from professional baseball
Run a brief exercise with a few of his players at practice
Have the general manager go over the program's purpose with him
rationales: Learning a coach's philosophy is usually where entry starts, but he has just laid it out and confirmed the consultant's summary. Asking again would look like not having listened.
A research summary suits a coach who asks what the evidence is. Dudek connects studies with a consultant whose work he never saw make a difference.
Entry should speak to what this coach counts as credible. With his aims understood, his remark shows that he judges by what players do, so a small, visible sample of the work fits him best.
Sponsorship helps when a coach doesn't know why a program exists. Dudek has been told; his doubt is about whether it changes anything on the field.
takeaway: Once a coach's aims are understood, build credibility in the currency that coach trusts.

stem: Before enrolling, all 30 volunteer coaches at a youth soccer club and the club's director agreed in writing to one rule for a consultant's coach-education program: whatever is used to judge a coach goes to the director, and whatever is meant to help a coach stays with that coach. Twice this season the consultant rated each coach's practice on the form the club uses to assign next year's teams, then met privately with the coach about things to work on. Now the director writes, "What should I expect from you?" What should the consultant send?
options: Each coach's ratings from the two practices, listed by name
Average ratings from the two practices, with names left out
A summary of what each coach discussed in the private meetings
A list of the coaches who completed both of their meetings
rationales: The form decides team assignments, so it is used to judge coaches and, under the rule everyone accepted before enrolling, goes to the director. Roles and information flow agreed at the outset should be honored as written.
Averages would protect coaches if the agreement had limited reporting to group results. Here they would withhold what the coaches knowingly agreed the director would have.
The meetings were about things to work on, so they were meant to help and stay with the coach.
A completion list suits an agreement to report participation alone. This agreement promises the director more than that.
takeaway: When reporting terms were clear and accepted at the start, carry them out, no more and no less.

topic: Naming the client in joint work
stem: A national federation gives each of its adult figure skaters ten hours with a consultant and wants only an invoice in return. The coach of skater Tove, who has trained her for six years, calls to book the hours. "We used to finish each other's sentences," he says. "Now I say one thing, she hears another, and we both go quiet." When the consultant phones Tove, she tells it much the same way: "I could talk to you alone, but then what? It happens when we're both standing there." As roles are set out, whom should the consultant name as the client?
options: The skater, with her coach consulted as needed
The coach, with his skater's views used as feedback
The federation, with skater and coach as participants
The pair, with both taking part on an equal footing
rationales: This suits a skater who wants help with her own skills or concerns. Tove says that the problem lives in what happens between them and that working alone would miss it.
This suits a coach who wants to develop his own coaching. He made the call, but he describes a shared pattern, as does she.
Paying for a service doesn't by itself make an organization the client. The federation has asked for no report and has no stake in the goals.
Both locate the trouble in their interaction and want to address it with the other present, so the relationship is the focus and the two of them are jointly the client.
takeaway: Identify the client from whose concern is being worked on, not from who called or who pays.

stem: Working from mastery-oriented coach training, a consultant watches an under-11 soccer practice with its coach. Lupe, who has been passing cleanly all week, rushes one and sends it wide. She groans, taps her ankle, and mutters, "Locked it too late." The drill moves on and the next ball is already rolling her way; she glances over at the coach, who says nothing. Afterward he asks the consultant how he might have responded to that pass. What should the consultant suggest?
options: Show her the correct technique once more
Encourage her and let the drill go on
Praise the technique she used on the pass
Remind her of the team's rules for drills
rationales: Corrective instruction helps a child who doesn't know what went wrong. Lupe named the error herself, so a demonstration adds little and slows the drill.
After a mistake, mastery-oriented training calls for encouragement right away. When the player already knows how to fix it, as Lupe's remark shows, encouragement by itself is enough.
Praise for technique fits a well-executed pass with an unlucky result. This one was rushed, she knows it, and praise for it would ring false.
Reminders of agreed rules are for lapses in conduct. Lupe made a playing mistake while trying.
takeaway: If a young athlete already knows the fix, encouragement alone is the best response to a mistake.

stem: A university women's rowing team rated how often they would prefer, and how often they see, four kinds of behavior from their new coach, Ulrike, on a 5-point scale. The average preferred and perceived ratings were 4.4 and 4.3 for training and instruction, 2.2 and 3.9 for democratic behavior, 3.1 and 3.0 for social support, and 4.2 and 4.1 for positive feedback. Satisfaction has slipped since she arrived, and the staff think the style the rowers want suits the season. Based on the multidimensional model of leadership, which change should the consultant suggest to Ulrike?
options: Teaching more technical detail during practice
Giving rowers more praise for good work
Taking more interest in rowers' lives off the water
Settling more of the training decisions on her own
rationales: Instruction is already within a tenth of a point of what the rowers want, so more of it would open a gap rather than close one.
Preferred and perceived positive feedback nearly match, so it isn't where the satisfaction problem lies.
The rowers see about as much social support as they prefer.

The one large gap is in democratic behavior, where the rowers see far more than they prefer. In Chelladurai's model, satisfaction depends on actual behavior matching preferred behavior, and that can mean doing less of something.
takeaway: Congruence cuts both ways: when athletes see more of a behavior than they want, leaders should offer less of it.

stem: A consultant is mediating between two esports teammates, Bao and Jasper, who have been blaming each other over voice chat. In the first half hour, each told how the blowups look from his seat, and each put the other's side into words until he heard, "Yeah, that's it." Since then they have been tossing out fixes: one of them always calls, they split the map, whoever has vision calls. There are seven ideas on the whiteboard, and the last two are the first two reworded. What should the consultant have them do next?
options: Choose one idea and decide how they will check it
Describe the problem and how it affects each of them
Restate each other's point of view to show they heard it
Come up with more ideas without judging any of them
rationales: Both sides have been heard, and repeats on the board show that new ideas have run out. Conflict resolution now moves from generating to selecting a solution and planning its follow-up.
Airing each side comes first in a mediation. They did this at the start, and going back risks reopening the blame.
Checking understanding comes before solutions. Each has already heard the other confirm that he was understood.
Brainstorming is valuable until it dries up. Seven ideas with repeats suggest that it has.
takeaway: Track where a mediation is in its sequence, and move forward when a stage has done its job.

topic: Parents who coach from the stands
stem: A consultant helped Coach Hadiya open the age-group swim season with a parent meeting, at which families talked through the roles of coach and parents and signed spectator guidelines they had drafted. Six weeks in, the bleachers are cheerful and the swimmers look to Hadiya before their races, with one exception. Before each of her events, 11-year-old Aino is called to the rail by her father, who whispers a race plan; last week she asked Hadiya, "So which one do I swim?" What should the consultant suggest that Hadiya do?
options: Hold another meeting on roles for all of the parents
Send all families the spectator guidelines in writing
Have a private conversation with the one father
Teach her swimmers a routine for focusing before races
rationales: A group meeting is the right preventive step and the right answer to a widespread problem. Here every family but one is following what was agreed.
Written guidelines help when expectations are unstated or forgotten. Families drafted and signed these, and nearly all keep to them.
Education of the group has worked for the group. A lone, repeated lapse is best raised by the coach in private with the parent concerned, focused on his child's confusion.
A refocusing routine suits distractions that can't be removed. This one comes from a parent whom the coach can speak with, and the other swimmers aren't distracted.
takeaway: Use group education for shared problems and a private talk for one parent's lapse.

stem: A consultant asks players on a high school girls' basketball team about their coach, Marcus Bell. "First in the gym, and he owns his mistakes." "He's got us seeing ourselves at state, and I actually believe it." "He figured out I learn by watching, so he sends me clips." In games, though, when an opponent switches defenses, five heads turn to the bench. "He'll tell us what to run," a guard explains. "It's his system, and it's a good one." Drawing on transformational leadership, which behavior should the consultant help Bell develop?
options: Living up to the standards he sets for the team
Asking players to question and improve what they run
Painting a picture of what the team could become
Fitting his coaching to what each player needs
rationales: Idealized influence is already present: players see him arrive first and own his mistakes.
Players wait for answers and treat the system as his. Prompting them to challenge assumptions and solve problems is intellectual stimulation, the component their accounts lack.
Inspirational motivation is already present: players picture themselves at state and believe it.
Individualized consideration is already present: he has noticed how a player learns and adapted to it.
takeaway: Match the development target to the transformational component that athletes' accounts leave out.

stem: Elite judoka Yusuf and his coach each complete a coach–athlete relationship questionnaire twice: once to give their own view, and once to guess how the other would answer. On a 7-point scale, all of their own ratings of closeness, commitment, and complementarity fall between 6.1 and 6.7. Their guesses about the other fall between 3.2 and 4.0 on all three. Training runs smoothly, yet each has privately told the consultant that he is "waiting for the other shoe to drop." Based on the 3+1Cs model, which activity best addresses the main issue?
options: Spending unhurried time with each other away from training
Writing down what they plan to do over the next three seasons
Hearing from each other how they really see the partnership
Agreeing on signals for giving and answering instructions
rationales: Shared time builds closeness, but both already rate their own closeness above 6.
A long-term plan shores up commitment, but both already rate their own commitment above 6.
Each feels strongly about the partnership and badly underestimates the other. The gap is in co-orientation, so the work is to bring their perceptions of each other into line with reality.
Signals build complementarity, but both already rate it above 6, and training runs smoothly.
takeaway: High direct ratings with low guesses about the partner point to a co-orientation problem.

stem: A consultant is helping a university men's lacrosse team share leadership more widely. Teammates agree that goalie Tevita runs the defense and fixes spacing on the fly, that two juniors lift everyone when the team is down, and that a senior midfielder is where players go to patch up quarrels. Over the fall, a booster dinner took place without a single player, the campus paper printed three players' conflicting accounts of one game, and the athletic director's office complained that it never knows whom to call. Which leadership role should the consultant help the team fill?
options: A task leader, who directs play and gives tactical advice
A social leader, who looks after relationships off the field
A motivational leader, who lifts teammates during games
An external leader, who represents the team to outsiders
rationales: The goalie already provides task leadership by running the defense and fixing spacing.
The senior midfielder already provides social leadership by helping teammates patch up quarrels.
Two juniors already provide motivational leadership.
The dinner, the newspaper, and the athletic director's office all involve people outside the team. Nobody holds the external role, though the task, social, and motivational roles are covered.
takeaway: Map athlete leadership roles against what is going wrong, and develop the one nobody holds.

stem: A consultant works with the coaches of a youth softball club. One of them, Marjolein, forwards an email she received this morning: "At the weekend tournament, Nell sat two innings of each game. The handbook says half of every game, unless I've misread it. Does that cover tournaments? No rush. I just want to tell her the right thing." The handbook, which Marjolein follows, has a separate line for tournaments. She has had a heated season with two other families and asks the consultant how to handle this one. What should the consultant advise?
options: Reply by email with what the handbook says
Set up a private meeting after a day or two
Cover tournament rules at the next parent meeting
Pass the email along to the club's director
rationales: This is a calm request for information that has a short factual answer. A prompt written reply respects the parent and settles it, whereas a bigger response would make a dispute of a question.
A cooling-off period and a private meeting suit an upset parent. Nell's parent is calm and wants a fact, so a meeting would raise the temperature.
A general explanation suits confusion shared by many families. Only one has asked, and that parent would be left waiting.
The director is the right next stop when a parent contests the rule or a coach's decision after speaking with the coach. This parent is doing neither.
takeaway: Match the response to the message: a calm factual question calls for a simple factual answer.

stem: A national-league women's ice hockey team gets a new coach midseason. The staff and the league's analysts agree that with a roster this young and a schedule this hard, detailed tactical teaching and firm direction are called for. On a preseason questionnaire, the players asked for loose practices and a large say in tactics. The new coach scripts each practice, stops play to teach, and makes the tactical calls herself, as she has done everywhere she has coached. Players follow her plans. According to Chelladurai's multidimensional model, which outcome is most expected if none of this changes?
options: Good performance and good satisfaction
Good performance and poor satisfaction
Poor performance and good satisfaction
Poor performance and poor satisfaction
rationales: Both outcomes are expected to be high when actual behavior matches what is required and what is preferred. Her style doesn't match what the players prefer.
Her actual behavior fits what the situation requires but not what the players prefer. The model links the first match to performance and the second mismatch to dissatisfaction.
This pattern is expected when the coach gives players what they prefer but not what the situation requires.
Both outcomes are expected to be low when behavior matches neither requirements nor preferences. Hers matches the requirements.
takeaway: In the multidimensional model, actual–required fit drives performance, and actual–preferred fit drives satisfaction.

stem: Paralympic wheelchair racer Wanjiru and her coach describe their work to a consultant. She says, "He's family. He says a word, I fix it; I ask, he's got an answer." He says, "Couldn't be fonder of her, and sessions run themselves." Each can say, correctly, what the other thinks about tactics, equipment, and training. But he has been answering calls from other squads, she has left his contract for next season unsigned on her desk, and both know it. "We take it a month at a time," she says. Under the 3+1Cs model, which aspect of the relationship most needs attention?
options: Commitment, their intention to stay together
Closeness, their trust in and liking for each other
Complementarity, how well their actions fit in training
Co-orientation, how accurately they read each other
rationales: His calls from other squads, her unsigned contract, and the month-at-a-time talk all point to weak intentions about the partnership's future.
Both speak of each other with affection and trust.
A word brings a fix and a question brings an answer, so their actions in training fit well.
Each knows the other's views, and both know about the calls and the contract.
takeaway: Commitment concerns the pair's intentions for the future, even when affection and cooperation are strong.

stem: A consultant is preparing a sales company's managers to lead ten-minute team check-ins built around a reset routine after lost deals. The managers have studied a guide and can give its steps and purpose from memory. Over two rounds of paired practice with feedback, they have covered each step, in order, in the flat tone of someone reading terms and conditions. "Is it meant to feel like a meeting?" asks one. "A pep talk? A chat?" Several others turn to the consultant, pens ready. The first real check-ins are in three weeks. What should the consultant do next?
options: Give the managers a fuller guide to the steps
Run another round of paired practice with feedback
Lead a check-in as the managers watch
Sit in on managers' check-ins with their teams
rationales: A fuller guide helps people who are unsure what to do or why. These managers already know the steps and purpose by heart.
More rehearsal helps people who know what they are aiming for. After two rounds the managers still don't know what a good check-in is like.
The managers know the content but have no picture of the performance, as their questions about its feel reveal. A live model gives them a standard to aim at when they practice again.
On-the-job observation suits managers who can lead a sound check-in and need support in carrying it over. These managers aren't there yet, and real check-ins are three weeks away.
takeaway: When learners know the steps but not what good looks like, model it before more practice.

stem: Vitali swam, ran, and played soccer and tennis until he was 12, kept soccer and tennis until he was 15, and gave up soccer last year because, he says, "I'd rather be on court." Now 17 and in good health, he hopes to play on the professional tour. His parents have read about the risks of specializing too early, and they ask a consultant whether his plan for the coming year should bring back other sports. Under the Developmental Model of Sport Participation (DMSP), which plan best fits him?
options: Several sports, with most time given to playful games
Two sports, with playful games and focused practice balanced
Regular activity for fun and fitness, without performance targets
One sport year-round, with most time given to focused practice
rationales: Sampling with plenty of deliberate play fits roughly ages 6 to 12, a stage that Vitali has already been through.
A balance of play and practice in one or two sports fits the specializing years, about 13 to 15. Vitali went through those with soccer and tennis.
The recreational path suits adolescents who want to stay active without pursuing elite performance. Vitali is aiming for the tour.
At about 16 and older, a young person who has sampled, specialized gradually, and chosen elite performance enters the investment years, marked by one sport and a high amount of deliberate practice.
takeaway: The DMSP warns against early specialization, not against investment by a committed older adolescent.

stem: Marit, a retired college gymnast now in graduate school, took up golf this month. Her teacher has read that mixed practice is best and has her change clubs and targets after each ball. In her second week, she makes solid contact on perhaps one ball in six, no two swings look alike, and she says, "I can't tell what I did, so I can't do it again." She has no plans to compete, and her body feels fine. She and her teacher ask a consultant to help plan her next few range sessions. Which plan best fits her stage of learning?
options: Switching clubs and targets from one ball to the next
Hitting one shot with one club in short blocks
Playing scored practice holes against a partner
Rehearsing the swing in her mind at home
rationales: Random practice strengthens retention and transfer once a learner can produce the movement. Marit can't yet, and this is the schedule she is lost in.
Marit is in the cognitive stage and has no basic pattern yet. Repeating one shot lets her form it; variety can be added once she makes fairly consistent contact.
Scored practice prepares a skill for pressure. Marit doesn't compete and has no stable skill to test.
Imagery works best with a clear model of the movement, and it can stand in when a player can't train. Marit is able to hit balls but can't yet tell what she did.
takeaway: Contextual interference helps once a learner has the basic pattern; absolute beginners may first need repetition.

stem: Collegiate dance major Nkechi has six weeks to prepare a 40-second solo. She learned its few steps in an afternoon. To polish it, she has been rehearsing it in three chunks, and each looks clean. Joined up, the solo dies: every turn has to spill into the next leap, and from a standing start at a chunk's edge she has nothing to spill. At half tempo she simply tips over. She asks a consultant to help her organize her rehearsals. Which plan best fits this task?
options: Dance the solo from beginning to end at tempo
Dance each chunk until it is secure, and then join them
Add one chunk at a time to those already joined
Dance the solo slowly, and then raise the tempo
rationales: The solo is simple but highly organized: each movement's momentum creates the next. Tasks that are low in complexity and high in organization are best practiced whole.
Part practice suits a long task whose sections are largely independent. Her chunks are already clean, and cutting the solo up is what breaks it.
Progressive-part practice suits a long sequence whose order or links are hard to remember. Her solo is short and well remembered, and stopping at a chunk's edge still kills the momentum.
Slowing a task simplifies it when it keeps its form at low speed. Hers depends on momentum and falls apart at half tempo.
takeaway: Practice whole when a task is simple and its parts depend on one another; use parts when it is complex and they don't.

stem: A consultant and a high school volleyball coach are planning a six-week program in which setters learn a refocusing routine at one session each Monday. In a trial run, the setters used every step well by the close of each session. "And then by the next Monday we're back to zero," the coach says. "Or it feels like that. I can't tell." Before they change anything, the two of them want one measure that will settle whether she is right. Which should they use?
options: How well setters use the routine as each session closes
How well setters use it in a match situation new to them
How well setters use it as each session opens, before review
How well setters believe they have learned it, rated weekly
rationales: Performance at the close shows acquisition. It was already strong in the trial and says nothing about what lasts until the next week.
A new situation tests transfer, and would fit if the question were whether the routine carries over to matches.
Best. The coach's doubt is about retention: what remains after a week without help. A check at the opening, before review, measures learning and not the temporary effect of practice.
Learners' judgments can show confidence, but they are a weak guide to retention, because ease during practice tends to inflate them.
takeaway: Learning is what remains after a delay: test retention before review, not performance at the end of practice.

topic: Planning for the stage of learning
stem: Halvard, a 52-year-old recreational triathlete, has been learning freestyle for three months. His stroke now looks much the same from length to length, and he no longer asks his coach what to do. Some lengths go better than others; after a poor one he often says, "Elbow dropped, I think," and looks to the coach to confirm it. If she chats with him as he swims, his timing slips. He asks a consultant to help him plan what to work on mentally in his next block of practice. Which plan best fits his stage of learning?
options: See the stroke shown again, and follow one or two main cues
Hold the stroke as he thinks through race tactics
Give his attention to each part of the stroke to rebuild it
Judge each length himself, and adjust on the next one
rationales: Demonstrations and a few simple cues serve the cognitive stage, when a learner is working out what to do. Halvard knows what to do and swims consistently.
Tactical thinking during movement needs the spare attention of the autonomous stage. Conversation still upsets his timing.
Conscious reworking is for a well-learned movement that has to be changed. His stroke needs refining, not taking apart.
A consistent stroke, growing awareness of errors, and attention still partly needed mark the associative stage. Practice there should sharpen the learner's own error detection and correction.
takeaway: In the associative stage, plan practice that builds the learner's own ability to detect and correct errors.

stem: A fire academy gives a consultant six hours to teach stress-management skills to its recruits. Last year all six fell on one day in week one, and the day went well: that evening recruits listed the skills without notes, matched them to sample calls, and used them in full gear in the training tower. At graduation, 12 weeks later, most couldn't say what the skills were. The academy can't add hours, but the consultant may arrange them in any way. Which change should the consultant plan for this year?
options: Have recruits pick among the skills on mixed sample calls
Split the teaching into short sessions across the course
Have recruits do more of their practice in full gear
Have recruits list the skills from memory as the day ends
rationales: Mixing skills builds the ability to choose among them, which recruits could already do on the day.
Recruits learned everything on the day and lost it over the weeks. Distributing the same hours over time produces far better retention than massing them.
Practice in gear helps skills carry over to working conditions. Recruits used the skills in gear on the day; what failed was memory.
Retrieval strengthens learning, but these recruits already listed the skills from memory that evening, and it didn't last.
takeaway: When learning is good on the day and gone weeks later, spread the same practice time out.

stem: Elite javelin thrower Chidi spent the off-season rebuilding his technique. By spring his coach no longer has to prompt him: film of his last 30 throws shows the new pattern each time, including when he is tired. Heading into the season, Chidi still goes down the runway reciting checkpoints. He tells the consultant, "I know it looks right. I have no idea whether it's doing anything." His early meets range from a small local event to a field of Olympians. Which goals would best serve him at those meets?
options: Distances to reach, set from his own recent throws
Technical points to carry out on each throw
Places to finish, set for each of the meets
An open aim of doing his best, with no numbers
rationales: The pattern is stable, and what he lacks is evidence that it pays. Self-referenced performance goals supply it whatever the field, and they move his attention off the checkpoints.
Process goals suit a pattern still being secured. His is secure, and more checkpoints would feed the recital on the runway.
Outcome goals can add drive, but with fields ranging from local throwers to Olympians, a placing would say little about his technique.
A do-your-best aim can protect someone learning a complex new task. Chidi is past that, and it would leave his question unanswered.
takeaway: Let the goal type follow the learning stage: once technique is stable, self-referenced results become useful.

stem: Collegiate swimmer Siobhan has done heart rate variability biofeedback for five weeks. With the on-screen display she holds her slow breathing pace for ten minutes. Last week her consultant hid the display. For the first two minutes she kept the pace and judged it within a breath of the sensor; then she sped up without noticing until the screen came back. No screens will be allowed on deck at her meets, which begin in six weeks. How should the consultant plan to use the display in the next few weeks?
options: Turn it off, and check her against the sensor at the end
Let her decide when she wants to look at it
Show it on some stretches and hide it on others
Keep it on through most of her breathing practice
rationales: Working without it is the aim, and would fit if she held the pace with the screen hidden. She still drifts after two minutes, so she would practice long stretches off target.
Learner-chosen feedback works when the learner can tell that she needs it. Siobhan drifted without noticing.

Best. She can feel the pace for a short time and loses it later, so feedback should be faded: enough to correct the drift, with growing stretches in which she must rely on herself. The guidance hypothesis warns that constant feedback would leave her dependent on the screen.
Frequent feedback suits the very start, before a learner has any inner sense of the target. After five weeks she has one, and more of the same would build dependence.
takeaway: Fade feedback as an internal sense of the skill develops: neither constant display nor sudden removal.

stem: For six weeks a consultant has stood behind elite archer Ilse in training and commented after each arrow on her pre-shot routine. Before each comment, Ilse gives her own verdict, and the two almost always agree. She says she enjoys the sessions and leaves them confident. Last week a late train kept the consultant away for the first half of practice. Her coach says that Ilse kept turning to look behind her and lost her place in the routine on nearly a third of her arrows; at Saturday's tournament, the same thing happened. What should the consultant change in training?
options: Comment in more detail on each arrow
Comment on fewer and fewer of her arrows
Comment mainly on the steps she does well
Ask for her verdict before commenting on each arrow
rationales: Detail helps an athlete who can't tell what is wrong. Ilse's verdicts match the consultant's, so she has the information already.
Her routine holds up only when a comment is coming. The guidance hypothesis explains this as dependence on frequent feedback, and the remedy is to fade it.
Positive feedback builds motivation and confidence. Both are in good supply.
Self-evaluation builds error detection, but she is already doing it, and accurately.
takeaway: If a skill holds up only when feedback is expected, reduce how often it comes.

topic: Explaining breathing to a young group
stem: A consultant taught slow breathing to a squad of 16- and 17-year-old gymnasts last week. They did it well, watched their heart rates drop on their wrist monitors, and agreed that it felt calming. None has used it since. "It's fine," says one. "It's what my grandma does in yoga." Another, who is taking advanced biology, adds, "I get that it did something. But breathing's breathing. Why would letting air out slowly do anything to nerves?" Heads nod around the circle. What should the consultant do next?
options: Make it a game, such as blowing out pretend candles
Have them breathe quietly and report what they notice
Show them their heart rates as they breathe
Explain briefly how long exhales act on the nervous system
rationales: A concrete image and a game suit young children. These are older adolescents who find the exercise a little childish already.
Guided noticing helps those who haven't felt an effect. They have done it and felt calmer.
A demonstration convinces those who doubt that anything happens. They have watched their heart rates drop and accept that it did something.
They accept the effect but can't see how it could work, and that question is keeping them from using it. Older adolescents can reason about mechanisms, and a brief rationale makes the skill credible.
takeaway: Pitch the explanation to the learners' development and to the question they are asking.

topic: Getting team skills onto the field
stem: In September a consultant taught a university women's soccer team several refocusing skills in weekly meetings. In November, with no warning, she asks players to write down what they remember. Nearly all of them explain every skill, and when she describes match situations, they choose sensible ones. Yet in matches she sees hardly any of it. "I know this stuff cold in here," says the goalkeeper. "Then I'm out there with my lungs burning and it's like I've never heard of it." Which change to the sessions is best supported by learning research?
options: Open with unannounced recall of skills from earlier weeks
Come back to each skill some weeks after teaching it
Move some of the practice to the field, at match intensity
Work on choosing the right skill for described situations
rationales: Retrieval practice strengthens memory, and their memory is strong: they explained every skill two months later.
Spacing guards against forgetting. They haven't forgotten.
The skills are well remembered in the room but don't appear under match conditions. Practicing under conditions like those of use, physical strain included, supports transfer.
Practice in choosing helps players who mix up the skills. They already choose sensibly.
takeaway: If skills are remembered but not used, make the practice conditions more like the performance conditions.

stem: The coach of a club wheelchair basketball team asks a consultant why his free-throw comments aren't helping the newest players. At practice, the consultant hears him speak up on about one shot in five, when something is well off: "Elbow's out." "Late release." He is just as quick to name what a good shot had in it. Players nod at the comments and repeat the fault. During a break, a newcomer demonstrates to a friend: "See, late. It felt late, too." She makes the same motion again and shrugs. What change should the consultant suggest to the coach?
options: Say what to do differently on the next shot
Comment on a smaller share of the shots
Point out more of what players do well
Show players video of their own shots
rationales: The newcomers can recognize the fault but don't know how to change it. Beginners need prescriptive feedback, which gives the correction as well as the error.
Cutting back helps when comments are so frequent that players depend on them. He speaks on one shot in five, and only for large errors.
Positive feedback is already there, and the trouble is a fault that persists.
Video helps players who don't believe or can't feel what the coach describes. The newcomer saw and felt it.
takeaway: Descriptive feedback names the error; beginners usually also need to be told what to do about it.

stem: A consultant has been teaching tactical breathing to police recruits. Three weeks ago they counted aloud and lost the rhythm if a door slammed. Since then they have kept it going while answering a radio, then with sirens playing and a stopwatch running, and, this week, in walk-through scenarios with role players. On the instructors' checklists, 22 of the 24 recruits held the rhythm in every walk-through, most of them talking as they did so. The training officer, remembering the slammed door, wonders what should come next. What should the consultant recommend?
options: Return to classroom practice until it is second nature
Use it in the full-speed use-of-force scenarios
Add a mild stressor, such as noise or a time limit
Switch to a simpler cue, such as a single word
rationales: Calm practice serves recruits who are still counting. These can breathe, talk, and act at the same time.
Recruits have kept the skill through progressively harder conditions, and with little conscious effort. The next step in a graded progression is the demanding setting it is meant for.
Mild stressors were the right step a couple of weeks ago, and recruits have since gone beyond them.
Simplifying helps when a technique is too much to manage. Nearly all of the recruits manage this one while talking.
takeaway: Raise the stress of practice in steps, and take the next step when the skill holds up.

stem: At a coach's request, a consultant looks into a high school volleyball team's serving. In practice, players hit 40 float serves to one zone, then 40 to another, and land about 90 percent. In matches the coach signals a zone before each serve. Going through match video, the consultant finds that players who are signaled the same zone twice running land nearly all of their second serves; after a change of zone, they miss close to half. Crowd size and score make no difference. Which change should the consultant suggest for practice?
options: Serving longer runs to a single zone
Serving with noise and a penalty for misses
Serving with a comment after each attempt
Serving to a different zone from ball to ball
rationales: Long runs help beginners get the movement. These players have it and perform at 90 percent in runs; it is the change that beats them.
Pressure practice helps players who falter in tense moments, but crowd size and score make no difference here.
Frequent comments help players who can't yet find the right form. Their form is good enough to land repeats.
Blocked practice lets players repeat a solution, but matches require building a new one for each serve. Random practice brings in that demand and improves retention and transfer.
takeaway: If a skill fails when the task changes, practice with the task changing from trial to trial.

stem: A youth hockey association asks a consultant to help coaches in its house league for 15- and 16-year-olds. Nearly all of the players left rep hockey a year or two ago, most of them after being told they would go no further. They skate on Friday nights; several also run or lift with friends. "I just like being out there," one tells the consultant. Yet the players have begun drifting away, and a typical session looks like a rep practice. Drawing on the Developmental Model of Sport Participation, which kind of session should the coaches run?
options: Playful games, drawn from several different sports
An even mix of hockey games and hockey drills
Mostly games and fitness, with few skill targets
Mostly drills on weaknesses, with close feedback
rationales: Sampling many sports through play fits children of about 6 to 12.
A balance of play and practice fits the specializing years, when players of about 13 to 15 are narrowing to a sport in which they hope to progress.
These players have chosen participation over elite performance. The model's recreational years stress enjoyment, activity, and health, with a good deal of deliberate play.
A high share of deliberate practice fits the investment years of players who have committed to elite performance. These players have left that path.
takeaway: In the DMSP, adolescents who aren't pursuing elite sport are best served by play, activity, and enjoyment.

stem: Professional concert pianist Sakura learned a concerto at 17 and has played it easily for 20 years. A conductor points out that she has been blurring two notes in one passage all along, because she crosses two fingers early. She agrees, and can play it cleanly if she stops to think. But as soon as she plays in her usual way, with her mind on the line of the music, the old crossing comes back, at home or onstage, rested or tired. The performance is seven weeks off. How should she practice the passage over the next few weeks?
options: Slowly, with her attention on each finger
At tempo, with her attention on the musical line
After a breathing exercise that settles her nerves
Within full run-throughs of the whole movement
rationales: Her automatic movement is the error. Changing it means bringing it back under conscious control for a time, and seven weeks leaves room for the new version to become automatic.
A holistic focus protects a correct automatic skill. Here it calls up the old crossing.
Calming down helps when anxiety disrupts a skill. The wrong note turns up at home and onstage alike.
Run-throughs help a passage that works by itself but not in context. This one goes wrong in both.
takeaway: Attention to mechanics disrupts a sound automatic skill, but it is needed for changing a faulty one.

stem: Professional esports player Tariq feels stuck and shows a consultant his practice log. Each block has a stated purpose ("hold angles after trades"), chosen from his most common errors. A coach reviews clips with him as each block ends, and the drills are set so that he fails about a third of the time. He practices from ten in the morning to ten at night with a sandwich at his desk, six days a week. The log shows reaction times creeping up from midafternoon, and by evening he is repeating errors he had fixed before lunch. Which change best fits deliberate practice principles?
options: A specific weakness to work on in each block
Feedback that comes sooner after each block
Tasks that go further beyond his present level
Fewer hours, with rest between the blocks
rationales: Each block already has a purpose chosen from his errors.
A coach already reviews clips as each block ends.
Failing about a third of the time already keeps him at the edge of his ability.
Deliberate practice takes full concentration, which can be kept up only for limited periods and depends on recovery. His decline through the day shows that he has gone past that limit.
takeaway: Deliberate practice is limited by concentration and recovery; beyond that limit, more hours add little.

topic: Recognizing warning signs in a runner
stem: In an initial assessment, collegiate distance runner Astrid asks for help with mental toughness because her times have slipped since fall, when her mileage went up by half. She has had two stress fractures since then, has not had a period for five months, and catches every cold. She is in bed by ten and wakes at seven, laughs easily, and looks forward to practice. "I'm not dieting," she says. "I eat exactly what I've always eaten." With her consent, the consultant arranges a visit to the team physician. Which concern do these signs most suggest?
options: Too little sleep for the training she is doing
Too little energy intake for the training she is doing
A depressed mood affecting how well she trains
A fear of racing that shows up in her body
rationales: Nine hours in bed, regularly kept, makes short sleep an unlikely explanation.

Missed periods, bone stress injuries, frequent illness, and falling times after a rise in mileage with no change in food suggest low energy availability (RED-S), which needn't involve dieting. A physician must evaluate it.
Easy laughter and looking forward to practice don't suggest low mood.
Race anxiety can produce bodily symptoms and falling times, but it wouldn't account for stress fractures and months without a period, and she looks forward to practice.
takeaway: RED-S can occur without dieting when training rises and intake doesn't; recognize the pattern and refer.

stem: A 17-year-old soccer player, Cormac, says he can't concentrate in class on Wednesdays and Fridays. The two-week sleep log he kept for a consultant shows lights out at ten and alarm at seven every day, weekends included, with his phone in the kitchen. He falls asleep within minutes except on Tuesdays and Thursdays, when he lies awake past one. Those are the days of evening training. "I'm dragging by then," he says, "so I grab a can of something at the station on the way. Gets me through." He doesn't snore and wakes rested after other nights. What should the consultant ask about next?
options: How much his bedtime shifts across the week
What he does on screens before lights out
How much caffeine he takes in, and when
How he breathes at night, and what his family hears
rationales: The log already shows the same bedtime and wake time every day.
His phone is in the kitchen every night, including the five on which he falls asleep quickly.
The trouble follows the evenings on which he has a can of something to get him through training. Late caffeine is the first thing to ask about before planning any change.
Loud snoring or gasping would call for a medical evaluation, but he doesn't snore and wakes rested after most nights.
takeaway: Let the pattern in a sleep log point to the next question before planning an intervention.

topic: Urgent signs after a head impact
stem: University rugby player Declan arrives for a first session an hour after a match in which he took a knee to the head. He tells the consultant that he was checked at the sideline, sent to rest, and felt "okay, just a headache." As they talk, the headache gets worse. He vomited twice on the way over, he answers more and more slowly, and he lays his head on the desk, saying he needs to sleep. The athletic trainer's office is a ten-minute walk away. What should the consultant do first?
options: Call emergency services and stay with him
Walk with him to the athletic trainer's office
Ask the team physician how to pace his sessions
Ask medical staff which return-to-play step he is on
rationales: A worsening headache, repeated vomiting, and increasing drowsiness after a head impact are red flags for a serious brain injury. The emergency plan comes first.
Prompt handover to the athletic trainer suits a suspected concussion in someone who is stable. Declan is getting worse by the minute.
Adapting sessions with medical guidance suits an athlete whose concussion has been diagnosed and is being managed.
Checking progress suits an athlete who is recovering under medical supervision.
takeaway: Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, or growing drowsiness after a head impact is an emergency.

stem: In early autumn, national-team swimmer Pilar, her coach, and a consultant map out a season that peaks at championships in August. General preparation runs through winter; specific preparation, with race-pace sets and small meets, fills the spring; a taper follows in July, and a transition period in September. Pilar learned a pre-race routine last season and can run it alone on an empty deck without a thought. At last season's one meet with it, she says, "there were people everywhere and a whistle, and it came out in pieces." Which phase should the plan make the main time for working on it?
options: General preparation, as volume builds
The taper, as the training load drops
Transition, once the season is over
Specific preparation, as racing begins
rationales: Early preparation is the time for learning a skill's basics. Pilar has them, and the phase offers few of the conditions that upset her.
In the taper, skills should be steady and familiar. Reworking the routine then would leave uncertainty just ahead of the championships.
Transition is for recovery and review, and it falls after the championships she is preparing for.
Her routine is learned but breaks down in racelike surroundings. Race-pace sets and small meets supply those conditions with time left to refine it.
takeaway: Learn skills early, adapt them to competition conditions in specific preparation, and leave the taper for rehearsal.

topic: Planning mental work in a taper
stem: Collegiate 800-meter runner Jamal and his coach are planning a two-week taper with a consultant. His log from the last three championship tapers reads much alike: heavy legs, fidgety, "can't sit through class," sleeping fine, imagery and routine done daily and enjoyed. Beside each he wrote a version of "here we go, right on time," and each ended in a season's best. The coach, who has just read an article on the psychology of tapering, asks what the consultant would like to put into this one. What should the consultant plan for the two weeks?
options: Keeping his present imagery and routine as they are
Teaching him what a taper feels like, and why
Adding a relaxation exercise to do in the evenings
Cutting back his imagery until the week of the meet
rationales: Jamal expects the sensations and reads them as a good sign, sleeps well, and has raced well on this preparation three times. A taper is for holding what works, so nothing new is needed.
Education helps an athlete who takes taper sensations for lost fitness. Jamal's notes show that he already reads them as normal.
An evening exercise would address trouble settling at night, and he sleeps fine.
A lighter mental load suits an athlete who is worn out by it. Jamal enjoys his daily practice.
takeaway: In a taper, keep what is working; normal sensations read well don't need an intervention.

stem: Elite biathlete Sigrun shoots nearly perfectly in dry practice. In races she skis hard into the range, and by her monitor her heart is at 90 percent of its maximum as she lies down; her best rivals' are, too. She means to get five shots away in about 30 seconds and can't afford longer. Video shows the rifle rising and falling with her chest as she fires. She sleeps well, starts races feeling sharp, and hits the first target as often as the last. Which skill should the consultant plan to build with her and her coach for the range?
options: Slow breathing at about six breaths a minute
A short pause after exhaling, timed to each shot
Progressive muscle relaxation from head to toe
Quick, deep breaths with an energizing cue word
rationales: Slow-paced breathing suits moments when the body is at rest. Six breaths would use a full minute and wouldn't meet the oxygen demand of near-maximal effort.
The rifle moves with her breathing, and neither her heart rate nor the time can change much. Firing in a brief pause at the end of an exhale steadies the rifle within both limits.
Progressive relaxation takes minutes and targets lasting muscle tension, which isn't what the video shows.
Psyching up suits an athlete who starts flat. Sigrun starts sharp, and her heart is at 90 percent of maximum.
takeaway: Fit arousal and breathing skills to the event's physiological demands and the time available.

stem: Snowboarder Kai, 15, rides carefully in training. When his friends film him, he goes for tricks that his coach hasn't cleared, and he has fallen hard. He and a consultant wrote if-then plans for those moments, and he rehearsed them daily. The coach cleared him a new set of tricks, which he lands easily and calmly. Three Saturdays later he recites the plan word for word and explains just how a bad landing can break a wrist. He also reports that he dropped it all three times: "Phones came out and I was already going." His friends say they are happy to film whatever. What should the consultant try next?
options: Going over the injury risks of the uncleared tricks
Rehearsing more if-then plans for when filming starts
Having friends film the runs his coach has cleared
Practicing a calming breath to take before dropping in
rationales: Information helps a rider who misjudges the danger. Kai can explain it in detail.
If-then plans are a good first approach, but he knows his by heart, and in the moment it has failed three times out of three.

In adolescence, peers heighten the pull of reward faster than self-control can answer it. Kai knows the risks and the plan, so the lever left is the situation, which his friends are willing to change.
A calming breath helps a rider undone by nerves. Kai is drawn in by the moment and rides calmly otherwise.
takeaway: When an adolescent's knowledge and plans give way in front of peers, change the situation.

stem: Over video, a consultant is teaching slow-paced breathing to Rosalie, a healthy sales executive, with a pacer set at six breaths a minute and a sensor showing her heart rate. She sits back with her shoulders low, and her belly moves gently. She doesn't feel dizzy. But near the end of each exhale her jaw tightens, and she snatches the next breath ahead of the pacer. "I'm running out of road," she says. When she slips ahead of it for a few breaths, the heart rate wave on the screen grows larger and smoother. What is the best adjustment?
options: Smaller, softer breaths at the present pace
Belly breathing in place of chest breathing
A break from practice until her physician is consulted
A pacer set slightly faster than the present one
rationales: Smaller breaths correct overbreathing, which shows up as large, forceful breaths with lightheadedness or tingling. Her breaths are gentle and she isn't dizzy.
Her shoulders are low and her belly is moving, so she is breathing that way already.
Medical advice comes first if there is chest pain, fainting, or a relevant condition. Straining at the end of an exhale is a matter of pace.
She strains at this pace, and her heart rate pattern improves when she speeds up. Best breathing frequency differs among individuals, so the pacer should move toward hers.
takeaway: Resonance breathing rates are individual; set the pace by comfort and heart rate response.

stem: Swimmers of 15 and 16 on a high school team get about six hours of sleep and nod off in class. At their coach's request, a consultant had them log two weeks. In nearly every log, the phone is out of the room by nine and the lights are off at half past; sleep comes around eleven, and the alarm goes at a quarter to five for practice. On Sundays, with no alarm, they sleep from about eleven until nine and wake rested. The coach has the pool from five until eight in the morning and may use any part of it. Which step is most likely to help?
options: Teaching the swimmers a wind-down routine for bedtime
Showing their coach how practice times fit teen sleep
Asking parents to have the house quiet by half past nine
Suggesting a medical evaluation of the swimmers' sleep
rationales: A wind-down routine helps teens who are on their phones late. These already put screens away and lights out in good time.

In adolescence the body clock shifts later, so sleep comes at about eleven whatever time lights go out. The wake time is what cuts sleep short, and the coach is the one who sets it and has room to move it.
Parents can help when evenings at home run late. The lights are already off at that time, and the swimmers don't fall asleep until eleven.
An evaluation suits a swimmer who is unrefreshed after plenty of sleep or who shows signs of a disorder. These sleep soundly and wake rested when allowed to.
takeaway: Teens' body clocks run late; when bedtime habits are sound, look at the wake time and who sets it.

stem: A consultant tracks professional cyclist Lucas with weekly mood and confidence ratings out of 10. Before a hard three-week block in February, his mood stood at about 8. It went to 7, 6, and 5 during the block, 5 after the recovery week, and 4 or 5 in each of the six weeks since, though his coach has kept rides short and easy. He still does his imagery and routine daily. His power is down, his sleep is broken, and he says, "Everything's fine at home, the contract's signed, and I'm just flat." Which reading of these data should guide the review?
options: A prolonged response that calls for medical evaluation
A planned dip that should lift with the next easy week
A reaction to events elsewhere in his life
A sign that the mental skills need to be changed
rationales: Mood, power, and sleep haven't recovered after weeks of light load. Planned overreaching should have cleared by then, so prolonged maladaptation or illness has to be considered, and that is for a physician to evaluate.
A dip in a hard block is expected and normally rebounds with recovery. He has had seven easy weeks without a rebound.
A mood drop that tracks life events would point here, but he describes home and contract as settled, and the drop began with the block.
A skills problem would show in how he uses them or in specific situations. He keeps up his practice, and the decline is general and physical.
takeaway: Mood and performance that stay low through weeks of light training call for a medical evaluation.

topic: Reviewing a plan during hard training
stem: At a quarterly review, masters rower Beatriz tells her consultant, "Maybe we need to rethink everything." She is 16 days into a three-week block that is her heaviest of the year. Her ergometer times are down by about 2 percent, her legs feel heavy, and she has been snapping at her crewmates. Her mental skills practice is as regular as ever, and she sleeps and eats well. Leafing through her log, the consultant finds nearly the same entry from the same week last spring, followed ten days later by "Legs back. Best piece of the year." What should the consultant suggest?
options: Seeing her physician about the drop in her times
Setting lower goals for the rest of her season
Keeping the plan, and looking again after the block
Trading some of her mental skills for new ones
rationales: A medical evaluation is called for when a decline goes on despite rest or comes with worrying signs. She is mid-block, hasn't rested yet, and has recovered from this before.
Goals should be revised when circumstances change. A short dip in a heavy block isn't a reason to expect less of the season.
A brief drop in performance and mood fits planned overreaching, as her log from last spring shows. The time to judge the plan is after she has recovered.
Skills are changed when a fair trial shows that they aren't working. Nothing here points to them; the cause is the training load.
takeaway: Don't judge a mental skills plan by data from the middle of a planned overload.

stem: A consultant has spent a season with a professional women's soccer team and wants to interview players about which parts of the program they used and why, to help decide what to offer next year. The last match, on a Sunday in October, will decide the title, and the coach wants nothing new asked of players before it. Four weeks of rest follow, during which staff are in the office; preseason opens in January. Eleven of the 24 players are on loan and fly back to their own clubs on the Wednesday after the match; by the team's habit, others leave for places without much signal. Staff won't have time to read the interviews until November. When should the consultant hold them?
options: In the week before the last match
During the four weeks of rest
In the opening days of preseason
In the first days after the last match
rationales: Interviews then would go against the coach's request before the title match and would miss the season's final test. The players will still be there afterward.
The transition is usually the time for analysis and revision, and staff will do that part then. By that point nearly half of the players will have gone to other clubs.
Preseason suits questions about the coming squad's needs. Loan players won't be back, and memories will have faded.
The whole season can be covered, all players are still there, and memories are fresh. Analysis can wait for the transition, but access to nearly half of the players can't.
takeaway: Collect perishable data while the sources are available; analysis can wait for the transition period.
